derives_from: **J.P.L. Gwynn's *A Telugu-English Dictionary* (OUP 1991)** for the letter-for-sound choices -- it is the standard modern dictionary of the language and its own headwords fix which letter an educated Telugu reader expects for a foreign sound (ఫ for /f/, జ for /z/, no nukta anywhere) -- and **the mechanism of `hi__hi-IN.json`**, which is Bhargava's page layout: hyphens dividing syllables, ordinary letters, a one-line legend, and the three-slot abugida pattern that decides where the virama goes. content/RESPELL-SYSTEMS.md names no Telugu pronunciation key and no published one was found; what is adapted is therefore stated rather than cited. The loanword spellings that decide the hard cases are Telugu's own and are checkable on any newspaper page: ఫోన్, బ్యాంక్, ప్లాట్ఫారం, జీరో, ఏటీఎం, వైఫై.

deviations.rule: Hindi's `ऑ`/`ॉ` for /ɔ ɒ/, and its borrowing of a letter for them
deviations.why: Not borrowed, because Telugu does not have to. Devanagari's inherent vowel is [ə] and its ओ is long, which leaves Hindi no letter for a short back rounded vowel and forces it onto ऑ -- a candra-o that IS Devanagari's own answer but is still an addition. **Telugu has ఒ/ొ, a short o with a dependent sign of its own**, and it is a closer match for [ɔ] than the borrowed letter. It is also the one override the derivation could not have done without: U+0911 and U+0949 shift onto U+0C11 and U+0C49, which are unassigned, and `shift_char` in tmp/te/build_respell.py raises rather than emitting them.

deviations.rule: Hindi's collapse of the four vowel-length pairs it cannot write
deviations.why: Undone, which is the largest thing this table does that the one it derives from cannot. Hindi maps /i/ and /iː/ both to ई/ी, /u/ and /uː/ both to ऊ/ू, /e/ /eː/ /ɛ/ all to ए/े and /o/ and /oː/ both to ओ/ो, because Devanagari has no short ए or ओ at all and its own short/long pairs stop at अ/आ इ/ई उ/ऊ. **Telugu writes all five pairs, with a dependent sign for both members of each** -- అ/ఆ ఇ/ఈ ఉ/ఊ ఎ/ఏ ఒ/ఓ -- so /i/ is ఇ/ి against /iː/ ఈ/ీ, /e/ is ఎ/ె against /eː/ ఏ/ే, /o/ is ఒ/ొ against /oː/ ఓ/ో. That is 24 phonemes whose length now reaches the page. `policy.length` is `none` for the same reason Tamil's is: the *script* carries the length, so the engine has nothing left to do with a bare `ː`.

**Refused, and this is the one place the improvement stops.** Short a has no dependent sign in Telugu any more than in Devanagari -- a bare consonant already says it -- so mapping /a/ to nothing would emit *nothing at all* in a nucleus, and every `aX` diphthong would lose its first vowel: Mandarin 好 /xɑʊ/ would come out with one vowel where the word has two. That is the exact defect `tmp/ta/nuclei.mjs` found in the Tamil table and paid for with eleven hand-written nucleus rules. So /a aː ɑ ɑː ə ɐ ʌ/ all take ఆ/ా, as in Hindi, and a Telugu reader gets a row one length-mark too long rather than one vowel short. A missing vowel is not a near miss; a long one is.

deviations.rule: Hindi's nukta letters फ़ and ज़ for /f/ and /z/
deviations.why: Dropped, and unlike Hindi's own §3.15.1 argument this is not a standards question: **Telugu has no nukta convention in use at all.** U+0C3C exists (Unicode 14) and is in neither the corpus nor the shipped face; every Telugu newspaper writes loan /f/ as ఫ and loan /z/ as జ -- ఫోన్, ఫారం, జీరో, జోన్ -- and Gwynn's headwords do the same. The shift would have landed on U+0C5E and U+0C5B in any case, both unassigned. The cost is the one Hindi names in the other direction: /f/ and /pʰ/ collide on ఫ, and /z/, /ʒ/, /dz/ and /ʐ/ all collide on జ with /dʒ/.

Replaced by the **ya-phalaka device**, `్యా` after a consonant and యా word-initially. Telugu's ఐ is unambiguously the diphthong [ai] and a reader would say it as two vowels; and Telugu already has a settled convention for exactly this vowel in exactly these words -- బ్యాంక్ *bank*, క్యాబ్ *cab*, ప్యాక్ *pack*, ప్యానెల్ *panel*, యాపిల్ *apple*. Bengali reached `অ্যা`/`্যা` independently for the same sound, which is two Brahmic scripts agreeing about a loanword rather than one table copying another.

approximations: Sounds with no Telugu letter, and what they get. Telugu's own inventory is large -- the whole four-way stop series, both retroflex and dental nasals, three sibilants, five vowel-length pairs -- so the list is shorter than Hindi's and every entry on it is inherited from that table rather than chosen here. /ʔ/ and /ʕ/ are written as nothing, which leaves a Thai zero onset correctly bare. /ħ/ is హ. /θ ð/ are థ ద, colliding with /t̪ d/ for the dental targets, which is the documented cost. /x ɣ q/ are ఖ గ క. /ç/ is ఖ where the target has an /x/ for it to front (German ich) and హ where it does not (Japanese ひ). /y yː ʉ ø œ ɵ/ are ఊ/ూ, Telugu's long u, which is how Telugu print reads a front rounded vowel (మ్యూనిక్, యూరో). /ɯ/ is ఉ, following the romanisation its two largest holders use -- Japanese u and Korean ㅡ. /ɤ/ is ఏ, which is what Telugu print gives Mandarin's e. /ɲ/ is న్య and /ʎ/ ల్య, Hindi's cluster shapes kept rather than replaced by Telugu's own ఞ and ఙ: **both letters exist and neither is written standing on its own.** ఞ appears in modern Telugu essentially only inside the conjunct జ్ఞ (జ్ఞానం, ప్రజ్ఞ) and ఙ only inside ఙ్క, so a bare ఞి for Japanese に would be a shape a reader has not met, where న్యి is one they read every day. Bare /ŋ/ is ంగ, the anusvara plus గ, which is exactly how Telugu writes an English -ing: మార్నింగ్. Vietnamese's glottalised codas and its /ˀ/ are dropped with the tone they belong to. /ʂ ʈʂ ʈʂʰ/ keep ష చ ఛ, since Telugu ష is a live letter with its own retroflex value rather than Hindi's ष, which Hindi speakers read as [ʃ]. Korean's /ɰ/ and Mandarin's /ɥ/ are వ and య.
note:
**Telugu is an abugida, so the design decision in this table is where the virama goes**, and it is Hindi's decision because it is the same problem: a consonant letter with nothing after it already says [a], so a cluster that forgets its virama does not merely look wrong -- it prints a vowel the target does not have. Every consonant therefore has three spellings and `spellSlot`'s position decides between them: bare when it is the first thing in the syllable (`after_out: ""`), so a vowel sign can bind to it; virama-then-letter anywhere else in an onset, joining it to the consonant before; and letter-then-virama in a coda, killing its own inherent vowel. The two directions are not interchangeable and a slot cannot look ahead within itself, which is why the choice is made on what has already been emitted.

**What Telugu adds to that mechanism, and what a reader should know before trusting the column.** The virama-then-letter form is not a sequence of two glyphs in Telugu the way it is in Devanagari: the shaper turns it into a *subscript* consonant hung below the line, so `్క` after a letter draws as a small క beneath it. There is no codepoint for any of the 36 subscript forms; they are reached only through GSUB. That is invisible to this table and load-bearing for the font build -- see TELU_RANGES in scripts/subset_fonts.py -- and it is why the `Telu` leading factor is 1.78 where Bengali's is 1.45.

**Tested the way the Hindi table was, by making the inherent vowel visible.** The claim to check is that no cluster prints a spurious inherent vowel, and the direct test cannot work, because a bare consonant followed by a bare consonant is *correct* wherever the target has an [a] there. So the table is regenerated with every inherent-vowel rule emitting a sentinel letter instead of nothing, and any remaining bare consonant-consonant adjacency is a virama the table forgot. **Over all 22,671 respellings the corpus can produce that count is zero**, and so are the four other invariants Telugu makes checkable: no vowel sign follows a virama, no two vowel signs land on one letter, no letter carries two viramas, and no syllable opens with a virama. tmp/te/shape.mjs, `SENTINEL=1` for the first.

**The `two signs` check is the one that found a real defect**, and it is why 64 of these rules exist. A Telugu consonant carries *one* vowel sign, so a vowel in hiatus has to take its independent letter instead -- Hindi's table carries that predicate by hand for the nine vowels it happened to need it for, and Devanagari has the identical defect on the rest. Vietnamese `biệt` /biɛ̯t̪/ printed `బిెత్` and `hryvnia` /…niə̯/ printed `నిా`, both with two signs stacked on one letter, until the predicate was generalised to every nucleus vowel. Neither `--gaps` nor `--units` can see either: every symbol had a rule and every rule was one somebody wrote.
